summary: Ken Pogran discusses how to give limited free access to file transfer servers, for example for mail, without assuming one particular scheme for access control. He argues that earlier proposals such as Bressler's in RFC 487 presume how authentication works, which different systems implement differently.

plainLanguage.summary: Many people wanted a guest door for sending files, and this author points out that every house has a different lock, so a single design may not fit all.

questions: principle of least privilege ftp server
subtitle: Ken Pogran separates access control, authentication and accounting to critique the free file transfer idea in RFC 487.

tldr.problem: Proposals for limited free access to file transfer servers, such as RFC 487, mix up controlling access to files, authenticating users and charging for resources, and they assume one particular way systems do these things.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC pulls the issues apart. It asks whose principal identifier the file transfer server runs under, who should be charged for transfers, and why a system-wide overhead account cannot be assumed.
tldr.outcome: It does not offer a replacement design. It asks the community to discuss how different systems really do authentication and access control before proposing network-wide mechanisms.

today: The unit metadata lists the status of RFC 501 as Unknown, and it is not marked as obsoleted or updated. It is a commentary on RFC 487, not a protocol specification.

sections.title: Three Issues Tangled Together
sections.content:
Ken Pogran of MIT-Multics observes that the ARPA Network is maturing and is now facing access control, user authentication and accounting. Proposals described as login-less mail, free accounts and free file transfer each embed some notion of how those mechanisms work, and implementors whose systems differ criticize them.

He singles out RFC 487, which he says muddles access controls on files with control of access to the system, and makes sweeping assumptions about accounting. The text of this RFC names the earlier proposal as RFC 467 in one place; the author means Bressler's free file transfer proposal. This RFC is deliberately only a partial discussion, with the rest left for later.
sections.plainLanguage: Getting into the building, opening a locked cupboard and paying for what you use are three separate things. The earlier idea mashed them into one.

sections.title: Whose Identity Does the Server Use?
sections.content:
In many systems, access control, file protection and accounting all meet at the moment a user is authenticated. The user, called a principal, gets processes tagged with an identifier and an account to charge.

The File Transfer Server can run in two ways. (1) As a system daemon with a highly privileged identifier, so it must itself work out what the user may access and charge the user's account. (2) With the user's own principal identifier, so the normal file system mechanisms check access automatically.

RFC 487 presumes the first. Systems concerned about protection may prefer the second because it follows the principle of least privilege: a process should run with as little access privilege as it needs. A footnote adds that such systems may require the USER, PASS and possibly ACCT commands before any transfer.
sections.plainLanguage: A helper can borrow your keys and only open your doors, or carry a master key to every door. The master key is riskier if the helper makes a mistake.

sections.title: Who Pays for Free Transfers?
sections.content:
The author questions charging a recipient for resources someone else used to send a file, comparing it to paying postage for junk mail. Letting an unauthenticated user say charge this to Bressler's account would require the server to be able to charge any user's account, which presupposes the daemon design. A more reasonable approach, he suggests, is to charge the server process to a general Network services account, with mechanisms presented in RFC 491.

He also challenges charging retrievals to system overhead. Such an account may not exist, may not be the right one, and would pass costs to local customers on hosts not funded by ARPA. It would also force the server to tell system file names from user file names, which many systems do not distinguish. Finally, he calls the claim that CPU charges are small naivete, since a busy host could accumulate a lot of CPU time over a week, month or year.
sections.plainLanguage: If a stranger borrows your phone, who pays for the call? The answer depends on whose plan it is, so a single rule cannot fit every phone.

sections.title: Push, Pull and the Wider Point
sections.content:
A footnote describes two ways to do the transfer Bressler wants: either the sender pushes the file with a User FTP to his system's FTP Server, or he pulls it with his User FTP from the sender's server. Bressler chose pushing, but since he wanted the file, pulling can be argued to fit better. A forthcoming RFC by Mike Padlipsky is said to expand on this.

The author's broader point is that network-wide mechanisms are hard to propose without building in assumptions about how systems implement them. He urges people to describe how their systems do authentication and access control so later proposals carry fewer assumptions.
sections.plainLanguage: Either the giver walks the parcel over, or the receiver goes to pick it up. The author thinks the person who wants the parcel should fetch it.
